title: Is there gravity on the space station?
hook: Astronauts float on the ISS. So gravity must be nearly gone up there. Is it?

knows: astronauts float on the International Space Station
doesNotKnow: that gravity falls off with the square of distance from Earth's centre
that floating in orbit is free fall

misconception: There is almost no gravity at the height of the ISS; that is why astronauts float.
objective: The learner can explain that at 400 km gravity is still about 88% of its ground value, and astronauts float because they and the station are in free fall together.

claims.text: Gravity weakens with the square of the distance from Earth's centre: g(h) = g0 x (R / (R + h))^2.
claims.source: Newton's law of universal gravitation for a spherically symmetric Earth. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 13.

claims.text: At 400 km, gravity is 88.5% of its ground value; at 6,371 km 25.0%, at 20,200 km 5.7% and at 35,786 km 2.3% (the far values the learner visited stay on a 'Seen:' row).
claims.source: (6371 / 6771)^2 = 0.885 (8.69 m/s^2); (1/2)^2 = 0.25; (6371/26571)^2 = 0.0575; (6371/42157)^2 = 0.0228. Checked in node with R = 6371 km. | REWORDED v3 (builder, 2026-10-14): Numbers unchanged; the reveal now quotes only the far stops the learner visited. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own node (R/(R+h))^2 with R 6,371: 88.53, 25.00, 5.749, 2.284 -> toFixed(1) 88.5%, 25.0%, 5.7%, 2.3%. 'Seen:' row lists stops index >= 2 the learner visited.

claims.text: The ISS orbits about 400 km above the ground; GPS satellites orbit about 20,200 km up and geostationary satellites 35,786 km up.
claims.source: NASA, International Space Station facts and figures (about 400 km, varies); GPS.gov, Space Segment (about 20,200 km); geostationary altitude from r = (GM T^2 / 4 pi^2)^(1/3) with T = 1 sidereal day: 42,164 km - 6,378 km equatorial radius = 35,786 km.

claims.text: Your 3 km/s (and/or 7 km/s) throw curved down and hit the ground (the × marks). The 7.67 km/s throw fell just as hard but kept missing the ground, on the station's orbit. Station and astronauts move at that speed, so they fall together. That is why they float.
claims.source: Apparent weightlessness in free fall; NASA, 'What Is Microgravity?' (NASA Knows!, 2017). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 13.6. | REVISED v2 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): Free fall is now shown on stage (decision 2026-10-14-told-vs-shown): the learner throws a ball sideways from 400 km at 3, 7 or 7.67 km/s and steps time; the reveal points at those traces. The slow-throw clause names only throws the learner made. Physics to check: same position and gravity for ball and station; 7.67 km/s = sqrt(GM / (R + 400 km)) is the circular speed, so a ball released at the station's speed shares its orbit. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own velocity-Verlet re-run of fly(): 3 and 7 km/s land; 7.67 km/s (sqrt(GM/6771) = 7.673) keeps r = 6771.000 km for 93 min, matching the station's circle (same start, same clockwise direction in Demo.tsx). Same position gives same gravity for ball and station (inverse square, no mass dependence). NASA 'What Is Microgravity?' not opened (nasa.gov blocked); secondary search-result text agrees (free fall, falling around Earth). Walkthrough transcript (08:21Z) predates v2 and shows no throw; checked against Demo.tsx only. | REWORDED v3 (builder, 2026-10-14): Wording trimmed; 'hit the ground (the × marks)' now matches the stage, which marks each landing with × and whose readout says 'falling, hits ground at N min' then 'hit the ground N km away'. Same physics as c7. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own velocity-Verlet re-run of fly(): 3 and 7 km/s land (× drawn where landMin !== null); 7.67 km/s (sqrt(GM/6771) = 7.6726) holds r 6771.000-6771.004 km for 93 min, same start and sense as the station. Slow-throw clause lists only seen.throws. Same position, same gravity (no mass dependence). Rests on simulation and Newtonian derivation, not on the unopened NASA page.

claims.text: 400 km adds only about 6% to the distance from Earth's centre.

At the far stops the stage draws Earth and the orbits to one scale; at ground and ISS height it zooms in, keeping Earth's radius and every angle true but stretching height above the ground about 6× (labelled 'Heights stretched 6×'). Earth is a round, non-spinning sphere with no air.
claims.source: Stated on stage ('To scale. Round Earth, spin ignored.'). Earth's oblateness and spin change surface g by about 0.5% (9.78 at the equator to 9.83 m/s^2 at the poles; WGS 84), small beside the effect shown. | REVISED v2 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): Added the zoomed-in view (same picture, same scale rule, smaller extent) and 'no air' for the throw model. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): near = k <= 1 zooms to the ISS orbit (NEAR_KPX), else to geostationary (FAR_KPX); chips 'Zoomed in, to scale. Round Earth, no air.' / 'To scale. Round Earth, spin ignored.' Model has no spin or drag. WGS 84 g 9.780 to 9.832 m/s^2 is about 0.5% (my knowledge). | REWORDED v3 (builder, 2026-10-14): v3 changes the near view from true scale to a radial stretch of height (HPX = 30 px / 400 km vs Earth 82 px / 6,371 km: 0.075 / 0.01287 = 5.8, shown rounded as 6). Landing angles are unchanged, so where each path lands is still to scale along the ground. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): DISPUTED. Code: far stops one scale (FAR_KPX), chip 'To scale. Round Earth, spin ignored.'; near stops E_PX 82 px for R and HPX 30 px / 400 km: stretch 5.83, shown 'Heights stretched 6×. Round Earth, no air.' True so far. But the radial stretch keeps only each point's direction from Earth's centre; it does not keep 'every angle' (a path's angle to the ground is drawn about 6× steeper). Learner-visible in the claims list. Fix (builder): 'keeping Earth's radius and each point's direction from Earth's centre true (so throws land where they really land)'.

claims.text: A ball thrown sideways from 400 km (no air) at 3 km/s lands about 961 km away after about 5.5 minutes; at 7 km/s about 5,176 km away after about 12.6 minutes; at 7.67 km/s it does not land: it circles once in about 92 minutes along the ISS orbit. Stage readout: 'T min: falling, hits ground at N min', 'hit the ground N km away' or 'T min: still missing'.
claims.source: fly() in Demo.tsx: velocity Verlet, 1 s steps, GM = 398,600.4418 km^3/s^2, R = 6,371 km, inverse-square gravity, no drag. Builder's separate node re-run gave landings at 5.45 min / 961 km (3 km/s) and 12.57 min / 5,176 km (7 km/s); circular speed 7.673 km/s, period 92.4 min. Newton's cannon: Newton, A Treatise of the System of the World (1728), fig. 'cannon on a mountain'. | REVISED v2 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. New stage behaviour and text. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own re-run, 1 s steps: 3 km/s lands at 5.45 min, 961 km arc; 7 km/s at 12.57 min, 5,176 km; 0.1 s steps give 960 km / 5,172 km (step size changes km by under 0.1%). Circular period 92.4 min. Readout strings match ballText. With 3-minute steps the 3 km/s readout first shows 'landed' at 6 min. | REWORDED v3 (builder, 2026-10-14): Readout strings updated only; the flight model (fly(), velocity Verlet, 1 s steps) is unchanged. Unverified. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own re-run of fly() (1 s Verlet): 3 km/s lands t 5.45 min (toFixed(1) '5.5'), arc 961 km; 7 km/s 12.57 min ('12.6'), 5,176 km; 7.67 km/s never lands in 93 min, period 2πR0/v = 92.4 min. Readout strings match ballText.

claims.text: One Earth radius up you were twice as far from Earth's centre, and gravity read 25.0%: a quarter. It weakens with the square of that distance, and 400 km adds only 6% to it.
claims.source: (6,371 / 12,742)^2 = 0.25 exactly; inverse square as in c1; 6,771 / 6,371 = 1.063 (c5). The first clause appears only if the learner visited the 6,371 km stop; otherwise the reveal says 'Twice as far from Earth's centre, gravity is a quarter.' | REVISED v2 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. Reveal now points at the 25% stop instead of only telling the square law (decision: inverse square acceptable, point at that stop). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): (6371/12742)^2 = 0.25, shown 25.0%; 400/6371 = 0.063. Reveal branch on seen.stops.includes(2) matches the source note.

recall.question: Why do astronauts on the ISS float, about 400 km up?
options: There is almost no gravity that high
They and the station are falling together around Earth
The station's air holds them up
recall.why: Gravity at 400 km is still about 88% of ground value; floating is free fall, shared with the station.
